items.title: Energy Department Order Takes Aim at Mid-Atlantic Blackout Risk
items.summary: The order as a precaution allows grid operators to use backup generation this week. There were no widespread outages reported.
items.full_text:
Title: Energy Department Order Takes Aim at Mid-Atlantic Blackout Risk - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/department-of-energy-emergency-power-order.html

Published Time: Wed, 14 Oct 2026 19:25:35 GMT

Markdown Content:
Power grids are vulnerable to wild swings in weather, from crippling winter cold to oppressive summer heat. But unseasonably warm early fall weather has energy officials taking steps this week to reduce the risk of outages in some parts of the country.

The Energy Department issued an order intended to make it easier for backup power to kick into gear in 13 Mid-Atlantic States and the District of Columbia, if needed, from Tuesday through Friday. On Wednesday, temperatures were in the upper 80s and 90s across a broad swath of the region, [National Weather Service data showed](https://graphical.weather.gov/sectors/midatlantic.php).

The order does not mean outages are expected or [that an emergency is imminent](https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/fact-sheets/pjms-emergency-procedures-and-messages.ashx). It is a precautionary tool, coming after a period of higher-than-normal temperatures in late August and September, as demand surged during the start of fall, when power plants are traditionally offline for maintenance.

The energy secretary, Chris Wright, said the order would help ensure Americans have “secure electricity by making additional power generation, including backup power, available to use as needed.”

## What prompted the order?

The emergency order was issued on Monday in response to an application by the grid operator PJM Interconnection, which coordinates the movement of wholesale electricity to at least 67 million people in Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia, as well as the District of Columbia.

“We’re sometimes called air traffic controllers of the power grid,” a company profile says.

The order gives the grid operator the authority to tap into backup generators, like those using diesel, to be used to support power grids if needed. Such a step would be taken before issuing a level 3 emergency alert, in which customers are asked to use less power or PJM takes other steps to avoid grid failure, such as by issuing rolling blackouts.

The emergency order allows PJM to direct data centers and other sites with high energy usage to switch to backup generators if necessary. It also provides “temporary relief from environmental permit restrictions for generating units,” the company said.

But the warmer days at the start of the fall season and into October are presenting a new challenge to grid operators. Demand for power is growing faster just as plants are usually taken offline, leaving fewer days for critical maintenance work.

“This is the new reality that grid operators are facing,” Jeff Shields, a spokesman for PJM Interconnection, said on Wednesday. “Planned maintenance season will continue to present risks that we formerly faced only in summer and winter,” he added.

## What does this mean for customers?

There were no reports of widespread outages. Utility companies usually keep customers informed if there are specific outages or ask them to reduce their power use.

Novec, which serves Northern Virginia, said on its social media account on Tuesday that crews were restoring power to a section of Prince William County, southwest of Washington, D.C., which has a population of about 500,000. It did not say what caused the outage.

The federal emergency order is not meant to signal to customers the need to take any precautionary measures.

Mr. Shields said the order represented a “last resort.”

“For perspective, the D.O.E. has issued a similar order at least nine times this year, and we have never had to use it,” he said. “It is another tool that we can use to protect the reliability of the system.”

## Social Security Says Retirees Will Get a 3.6% Raise for 2027

The cost of living adjustment, or COLA, for next year will be the largest since 2023. Retirees will see the extra money in their benefit checks starting in January.

Listen

· 7:25 min

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14biz-ss-cola-qlfw/14biz-ss-cola-qlfw-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A Social Security Administration office in Jamaica, Queens. Credit...Dave Sanders for The New York Times

By Mark Miller

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 10:31 a.m. ET

Retirees and other beneficiaries will receive the largest annual cost-of-living adjustment since 2023 in their Social Security checks next year, driven mainly by [persistently high inflation](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/14/business/inflation-cpi-report-september).

The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6 percent annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, on Wednesday after the release of government inflation data for September. The COLA is determined using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The index values for July, August and September are averaged to produce the official adjustment figure.

For the average Social Security beneficiary, the COLA will translate to a $75 monthly increase, the government said. However, the actual amount for any retiree enrolled in Medicare will vary. The Part B premium, which covers outpatient care, is usually deducted from Social Security benefits, changing net COLAs. Separately, Social Security said the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax would rise to$192,300, up from $184,500 this year.

The Medicare board of trustees has projected that the monthly Part B premium will rise $6.60 in 2027 to $209.50. The final figure will be released this fall, but if the projection holds, most beneficiaries will receive net COLAs of at least 3 percent.

Other Medicare costs are rising, too. Monthly premiums for some [prescription drug plans](https://www.kff.org/medicare/many-medicare-part-d-stand-alone-drug-plan-enrollees-will-see-modest-premium-increases-for-2027-but-others-could-pay-much-more-if-they-dont-switch-plans/), which are known as Part D, will jump $50 or more next year — although plenty of lower-cost options are available for people who shop the market during the annual enrollment period that begins Thursday. In addition, [costs will rise](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/medicare-private-health-care-costs.html) and supplemental benefits will be reduced in private Medicare Advantage plans next year.

The CPI-W reflects price changes for goods and services that working people buy and use, and it is under-weighted for health care costs, which have an outsize impact on older Americans. The health spending burden for people enrolled in Medicare is more than twice as large as that of other households, accounting for [14 percent of total spending](https://8cmbykf0.r.us-east-1.awstrack.me/L0/https:%2F%2Fwww.kff.org%2Fmedicare%2Fkey-facts-about-health-care-affordability-for-people-with-medicare%2F/1/010001a1311a1da5-c40d42ca-9c53-4371-a8d1-c36eb1de8306-000000/YNSLf9mYyKWQ9lu1aZkteiU1d_M=473) in 2024, according to KFF, a health care research nonprofit.

items.title: Senators Question Meta’s Data Center Tax Strategy
items.summary: Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee sent a letter to Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, questioning the company’s $6.6 billion in tax breaks.
items.full_text:
Title: Senators Question Meta’s Data Center Tax Strategy - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/technology/meta-senators-tax-avoidance.html

Published Time: Wed, 14 Oct 2026 19:12:51 GMT

Markdown Content:
Lawmakers on the Senate Finance Committee on Tuesday accused Meta of a “violation of the spirit and, potentially, the letter of the tax law” for shaving billions of dollars off its federal tax bill using a tax credit intended to boost research and experimentation.

In [a letter to Mark Zuckerberg](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/14/us/senate-letter-to-meta-on-research-tax-credit.html), Meta’s chief executive, seven Democratic senators, including Ron Wyden of Oregon, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, asked the company about $6.6 billion worth of federal research tax credits the company has claimed over the last two years.

The letter follows a [New York Times report](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/technology/meta-ai-data-centers-taxes.html) last month that Meta has claimed to the Internal Revenue Service that the data centers it is building across the country to power its new generative A.I. efforts are “experimental.” The strategy raised concern within the company’s finance team because the credit is not supposed to be applied to supplies used in standard business operations.

Since it began applying the credit to the costs of its A.I. data centers and their expensive computer chips, Meta has become the largest claimant of the research tax credit in the United States, using it to knock off nearly $4 billion from its tax bill last year, and $2 billion the year before.

Tax experts told The Times that the credit is intended for projects that have technical uncertainties and might fail, such as the mini data center on a satellite that Google is [sending to space](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/technology/google-suncatcher-ai-data-center-space.html). Meta’s characterizing the A.I. data centers it is building on thousands of acres across the country as experimental is “kind of wild and out there,” Andre Shevchuck, a partner at the tax advisory firm BPM, told The Times.

In the letter to Mr. Zuckerberg, the senators asked Meta for the accounting behind the company’s tax break, and how much it has claimed for the purchase of “microchips, computing equipment and other materials necessary to build or operate A.I. data centers.” The senators also inquired about a $355 million tax break the company took a decade ago on Mr. Zuckerberg’s compensation, by claiming that he was a researcher.

Andy Stone, a company spokesman, said that Meta has invested $200 billion in research and development over the last five years.

“Unlike traditional data centers, A.I.-optimized data centers are inherently new and require extensive testing and experimentation that cannot be simulated in order to get the design and build right,” he said. “This is precisely the kind of domestic investment Congress encouraged when it established these tax incentives decades ago.”
